deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files From an Internal Hard Drive
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files on a hard drive are often still there until overwritten. Learn how to stop the damage and safely recover them with free tools like PhotoRec.
deleted.summary: When you delete a file, the computer usually just marks its space as free. The data stays on the disk until something new is written over it. The sooner you stop using the drive, the better your chances.
deleted.riskNote: The drive is healthy, so recovery only reads data, as long as you save results to a different drive.
stopFirst: Stop saving, downloading, installing or browsing on this drive right now. New data can overwrite your deleted files.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive. Install it on a different drive or run it from a USB stick.
Do not save recovered files back to the same drive. Always pick a different drive.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: If it is your Windows or Mac system drive, shut down now. Every minute the computer runs, it writes small files that can overwrite what you deleted.

steps.title: Check the Recycle Bin or Trash first
steps.detail: Open the Recycle Bin (Windows) or Trash (Mac). If your file is there, restore it and you are done. Also check cloud backups or File History and Time Machine.

steps.title: Prepare a second drive
steps.detail: Get a separate drive with enough free space to hold everything you want back. This is where recovered files will be saved.

steps.title: Run recovery from another computer or a USB stick
steps.detail: Best is to connect the drive to a second computer, or boot from a USB stick with TestDisk and PhotoRec. This keeps the original drive untouched.

steps.title: Try TestDisk first for whole folders
steps.detail: TestDisk can often list deleted files with their original names and folders. Copy what you need to your second drive.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if names are lost
steps.detail: PhotoRec scans for file types such as photos and documents. It brings back the contents, but file names and folders are usually gone, so you sort them afterwards.

steps.title: Check your recovered files
steps.detail: Open a sample of files to be sure they work. Keep the original drive unchanged until you are happy with the results.

deleted.callPro: If the drive starts making odd noises, disappears, or the files are very valuable and recovery fails, stop and talk to a professional before trying more.

faq.q: Can I get back files I emptied from the Recycle Bin?
faq.a: Often yes. Emptying the bin only frees the space. Recovery works if nothing new has overwritten it, so stop using the drive right away.

faq.q: Why did my recovered files lose their names?
faq.a: PhotoRec finds files by their content, not by the file table, so names and folders are not saved. TestDisk can sometimes keep names if the file table is still intact.

faq.q: Is it a problem that I kept using the computer after deleting?
faq.a: It lowers the odds a bit, because new data may land on the freed space. Stop now and recover what is left.

formatted.title: Recover Files From a Formatted Hard Drive
formatted.metaDescription: Accidentally formatted a hard drive? Quick format is often recoverable, full format on Windows is not. Learn what to do and which free tools to use.
formatted.summary: A quick format wipes the drive's table of contents but leaves most of your data in place, so recovery is often possible. A full format on modern Windows (Vista and later) writes zeros over everything, and that data is gone for good.
formatted.riskNote: Software recovery only reads from the drive, but writing anything new to it can destroy what is left.
stopFirst: Do not copy, save or install anything onto the formatted drive. New data overwrites what you want back.
Do not format it again, and do not reinstall the operating system on it.
Do not install recovery software onto the formatted drive. Use a different drive.

steps.title: Work out which kind of format you did
steps.detail: A quick format finished in seconds or minutes. A full format ran for a long time. On Windows Vista and later, a full format writes zeros, so the old data cannot be brought back.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: If it was your system drive and you reinstalled the operating system, the new install has already overwritten some data. Stop and do not install anything else.

steps.title: Attach it to a second computer
steps.detail: Connect the drive as a secondary drive, or boot from a USB stick with recovery tools. Prepare a separate drive with enough space to save results.

steps.title: Try TestDisk to restore the old structure
steps.detail: TestDisk can search for the lost partition and may bring back folders with their original names. This works best after a quick format.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if TestDisk finds nothing
steps.detail: PhotoRec scans the whole drive for known file types and saves them to your second drive. Names and folders are usually lost, but the content is back.

steps.title: Check what you got
steps.detail: Open a few files of each type. If many are damaged or missing, the drive may have been fully formatted or overwritten.

formatted.callPro: If the drive is making noises, is not detected, or the data is critical and software scans fail, stop and consult a professional.

faq.q: Can I recover data after a full format?
faq.a: On Windows Vista and newer, a full format writes zeros over the disk, so the data is gone. A quick format is a very different story and is often recoverable.

faq.q: Did reinstalling Windows destroy my files?
faq.a: It overwrote part of the drive, so some files are lost. Others may still be recoverable, so stop and scan with PhotoRec.

faq.q: Will I get my folders and file names back?
faq.a: Sometimes with TestDisk. With PhotoRec, files usually come back with generic names and are sorted by type.

not-detected.title: Hard Drive Not Showing Up or Not Detected
not-detected.metaDescription: Hard drive not detected or not showing in Windows or Mac? Check cables, ports and Disk Management first, then recover data without more damage.
not-detected.summary: A drive that does not show up may have a loose cable, a bad port, a lost partition, or a real hardware fault. The first checks are simple and safe. If the drive is silent, clicking, or hot, the cause may be physical.
not-detected.riskNote: Cable and software checks are safe, but repeated power-ups of a physically failing drive can make the damage worse.
stopFirst: Do not keep powering the drive on and off to see if it comes back. Each attempt can add wear if it is failing.
Do not click Initialize or Format if your computer offers it. That can erase the data.
Do not open the drive. Hard drives need a cleanroom, and dust ruins them.

steps.title: Listen and feel
steps.detail: A healthy drive spins up with a soft hum. If you hear clicking, grinding or beeping, or smell something burnt, stop here and read the clicking guide instead.

steps.title: Check the BIOS or UEFI
steps.detail: Restart and open the BIOS screen. If the drive is listed there, the hardware is talking to the computer and the problem is likely software or partition related.

steps.title: Swap the cable and port
steps.detail: Try a different SATA data cable and a different port, and check the power connector. Bad cables cause many drive-not-found problems.

steps.title: Look in Disk Management or Disk Utility
steps.detail: On Windows, open Disk Management. On Mac, open Disk Utility. If the drive is listed but has no letter or says Raw or Unallocated, do not format it.

steps.title: Check drive health
steps.detail: Use CrystalDiskInfo on Windows or smartmontools on Linux or Mac to read the SMART health report. Warnings like Caution or Bad mean the drive is failing.

steps.title: Copy the data off or make an image
steps.detail: If the drive is readable but weak, make an image with ddrescue onto another drive first. Then use TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image, not the original.

steps.title: Stop if it still does not appear
steps.detail: If it is not seen in the BIOS after a cable swap, the drive or its circuit board has likely failed. Further DIY is risky.

not-detected.callPro: If the drive is missing from the BIOS after trying a new cable and port, or it makes any unusual noise, stop and consider a professional with a cleanroom.

faq.q: My drive shows up but says Raw or needs formatting. What now?
faq.a: Do not format it. The file table may be damaged, and TestDisk or PhotoRec can often still reach your files.

faq.q: Could it just be a cable?
faq.a: Yes, that is very common. Try another cable, port, and power connector before assuming the drive is dead.

faq.q: Can I fix it by swapping the circuit board?
faq.a: Not reliably. Boards hold drive-specific data, and a mismatched board can make things worse. It is best left to specialists.

clicking.title: Hard Drive Clicking, Grinding or Beeping
clicking.metaDescription: A clicking, grinding or beeping hard drive is failing mechanically. Learn what not to do, why the freezer trick is a myth, and when DIY is reasonable.
clicking.summary: Clicking, grinding or beeping usually means the moving parts inside, such as the read/write heads, are damaged or stuck. Every extra power-up can scratch the disk surface and destroy more data.
clicking.riskNote: Mechanical faults can get worse every time the drive is powered on, and real repairs need a cleanroom.
stopFirst: Power it off and leave it off. Do not keep trying, because each power-up can scratch the platters.
Do not put the drive in the freezer, tap it, or shake it. The freezer trick is a myth that can cause condensation damage.
Never open the drive. Dust in a normal room ruins the platters.
Do not run recovery software or repair tools on it. Heavy scanning stresses a failing drive.

steps.title: Unplug it now
steps.detail: Shut down and disconnect the drive. Note what you heard (clicking, grinding, beeping, or not spinning) because it helps when talking to an expert.

steps.title: Decide how valuable the data is
steps.detail: If it is irreplaceable, the safest choice is a professional lab with a cleanroom. If it is replaceable or you accept the risk, read on.

steps.title: Check for easy causes
steps.detail: Make sure the clicking is from the drive and not a fan. Try a different power connector or cable once, in case low power is the cause.

steps.title: Try one careful attempt, if you accept the risk
steps.detail: Connect it to a computer that is not booting from it. If it spins up and appears, immediately start imaging with ddrescue or HDDSuperClone onto a different healthy drive.

steps.title: Image, don't copy
steps.detail: ddrescue first reads the easy parts and skips the bad areas, so the most data is saved before the drive gets worse. Be ready to stop if it clicks again.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Once you have an image, run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image file, never on the original failing drive.

steps.title: Stop at the first sign of trouble
steps.detail: If it clicks, stalls, or disappears again, power it off. Further attempts lower the odds for a professional.

clicking.callPro: If the data matters and the drive clicks, grinds, beeps or will not spin, stop and have a professional with a cleanroom look at it.

faq.q: Does the freezer trick work?
faq.a: No. It can cause condensation and make the damage worse. Experts and data recovery communities advise against it.

faq.q: Can I open the drive and fix it myself?
faq.a: No. Opening a hard drive outside a cleanroom lets in dust that can scratch the platters. Head replacement needs special tools and matching parts.

faq.q: Is it worth trying once myself?
faq.a: It can be if the data is not critical, but keep it to one or two careful attempts and image the drive immediately if it works.

no-power.title: Hard Drive Not Spinning or Won't Power On
no-power.metaDescription: Hard drive silent, not spinning, or smells burnt? Check power and cables safely, learn why not to retry again and again, and when to see a professional.
no-power.summary: If the drive makes no sound and does not spin, the cause may be a bad cable, bad power supply, or a failed circuit board or motor. A burnt smell suggests an electrical fault, which can be dangerous to keep trying.
no-power.riskNote: Simple cable and power checks are fine, but repeated attempts on a drive with a burnt board or stuck motor can cause more harm.
stopFirst: Unplug it right away if you smell burning or see scorch marks. Do not power it up again.
Do not power-cycle it again and again hoping it starts. Limit yourself to one or two careful tries.
Do not use the freezer trick, and never open the drive. It needs a cleanroom.
Do not swap circuit boards yourself. Boards hold drive-specific data and mismatches cause problems.

steps.title: Look and smell
steps.detail: Check the circuit board on the underside for burn marks, a burnt chip, or a burnt smell. If you see or smell any, leave it unplugged.

steps.title: Test the power source
steps.detail: Try a different power connector, a different SATA power cable, or a different computer. A weak power supply is a common cause.

steps.title: Try another cable and port
steps.detail: Swap the data cable and the port. If the drive is in a desktop, check that other drives get power from the same cable.

steps.title: Listen for spin-up
steps.detail: Rest your hand lightly on the drive when you power it on. A faint hum or vibration means it spins. Silence means a power, board or motor issue.

steps.title: If it spins and shows up, image it
steps.detail: Use ddrescue or HDDSuperClone to copy it to a different drive. Do not install software on the affected drive.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image file, not the original.

steps.title: Stop if it stays dead
steps.detail: A drive that never spins needs hardware repair by a professional. More attempts will not help.

no-power.callPro: If it does not spin after trying another cable and power source, or there is a burnt smell or scorch marks, stop and use a professional.

faq.q: My drive is dead but not clicking. Is that better or worse?
faq.a: Neither is good. Silence points to power, circuit board or motor trouble. Check the cable and power first, then consider a professional.

faq.q: Can I replace the circuit board myself?
faq.a: It is risky. Modern boards hold unique adaptive data, so a swap often fails unless that data is moved too. Experts do this with special tools.

faq.q: Is a burnt smell always the end?
faq.a: Not always. Sometimes only the protection part on the board has blown and the data is fine, but it needs a careful repair by an expert.

liquid-fire.title: Water, Liquid or Fire Damaged Hard Drive
liquid-fire.metaDescription: Hard drive got wet, flooded or burned? Do not power it on, do not use rice or heat. Learn what to do next to give a professional the best chance.
liquid-fire.summary: Liquid can short the circuit board and corrode parts inside, and fire or heat can warp the drive. Powering it on can cause a short or scratch the platters, so the safest move is to keep it off and get professional help.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Power, heat, or opening the drive can turn recoverable damage into permanent loss.
stopFirst: Do not power it on. Not even once to see if it works.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven, or heater, and do not bury it in rice. Heat and rice make corrosion and dust worse.
Do not open the drive or try to clean the platters.
Do not shake it or rinse it to remove dirt or salt water.

steps.title: Keep it unpowered
steps.detail: Unplug it and leave it off. Turning it on while wet can cause a short that fries the board or scratches the disk.

steps.title: Note what happened
steps.detail: Was it clean water, salt water, a sugary drink, flood mud, smoke or flames? This matters, because salt and mud corrode quickly.

steps.title: Keep it damp if it came from a flood
steps.detail: If it is muddy or salty, sealing it in a sealed bag with a little of the same water can slow corrosion until an expert sees it. Do not let it dry out in the open.

steps.title: Pack it gently
steps.detail: Wrap it in a soft cloth, put it in a box with padding, and avoid bumps or heat.

steps.title: Contact a professional soon
steps.detail: Corrosion keeps spreading with time, so do not wait. Choose a lab that works in a cleanroom and ask about their policy before you pay.

steps.title: Only if the data is not critical
steps.detail: If the drive was only splashed and is fully dry after several days, some people try one careful power-up with a spare cable. Be aware this can destroy it, and stop at the first odd sound.

liquid-fire.callPro: Water, liquid, smoke or fire damage should go to a professional with a cleanroom before anyone powers the drive on.

faq.q: Will putting it in rice help?
faq.a: No. Rice does not pull water out of a drive, and it can add dust and starch. Keep it off and get professional help.

faq.q: Can I dry it with a hair dryer?
faq.a: No. Heat can warp parts and drive moisture further inside. Leave drying and cleaning to an expert.

faq.q: What if it was fully dry and looks fine?
faq.a: Looking fine is not proof it is safe, because residue can short the board. Powering it is a gamble, so a professional is safer for important data.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted or Unreadable Hard Drive
corrupted.metaDescription: Hard drive corrupted, shows RAW, asks to format, or has read errors? Image it with ddrescue first, then recover files with TestDisk or PhotoRec safely.
corrupted.summary: Corruption means the drive's file records are damaged, often after a power loss, a bad shutdown, or failing sectors. The files may still be there. Do not run repair tools on the original first, because they can change data.
corrupted.riskNote: The drive may be weakening, and repair tools like CHKDSK on the original can change data before you have a copy.
stopFirst: Do not run CHKDSK, fsck, or Disk Utility repair on the original before copying your data. Repairs can rewrite data.
Do not click Format when Windows says the drive needs to be formatted.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive, and do not save recovered files back to it.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Shut down or unmount it. If it is making noises, read the clicking guide instead.

steps.title: Check its health
steps.detail: Use CrystalDiskInfo (Windows) or smartmontools to read the SMART report. Reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sectors mean the disk is wearing out.

steps.title: Get a second drive that is as large
steps.detail: You need a different drive at least as big as the damaged one to hold an image of it.

steps.title: Image the drive with ddrescue
steps.detail: GNU ddrescue copies the drive to a file or another drive, skipping unreadable spots and coming back to them later. HDDSuperClone is an alternative. Save the log file so you can resume.

steps.title: Work on the image, not the original
steps.detail: Make a copy of the image if you can. Then run TestDisk to rebuild partitions or restore folders, on the image only.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec as a fallback
steps.detail: If the folder structure is too damaged, PhotoRec carves out files by type from the image. Names will be generic.

steps.title: Store the recovered files safely
steps.detail: Save to a third location if you can, and check that the files open correctly.

corrupted.callPro: If imaging keeps stalling, the drive makes noises, or the data is critical, stop and talk to a professional rather than hammering the drive.

faq.q: Should I run CHKDSK to fix it?
faq.a: Not first. It can rewrite damaged data. Make an image of the drive, then repair or recover from that copy.

faq.q: What is a disk image?
faq.a: It is an exact copy of everything on the drive saved as a file or onto another drive. It lets you try recovery over and over without risking the original.

faq.q: Why does it say the drive is RAW?
faq.a: The computer cannot read the file system, usually due to damage. The data is often still there and TestDisk may restore it.

encrypted.title: Recover Data From an Encrypted Hard Drive
encrypted.metaDescription: Locked out of a BitLocker, FileVault or other encrypted hard drive? Find your recovery key first. Without the key or password, recovery is not realistic.
encrypted.summary: Encryption scrambles your data so that only the right password or recovery key can unlock it. If the drive is healthy and you have the key, getting files back is usually simple. Without it, recovery is not realistic, and anyone promising otherwise should not be trusted.
encrypted.riskNote: Unlocking with a known key is low risk, but guessing or tampering with a failing encrypted drive can lock you out for good.
stopFirst: Do not format, reset, or reinstall the operating system. That destroys the encryption headers and your chance of unlocking.
Do not keep guessing passwords on a drive that locks you out after failed tries.
Do not trust tools or sites that claim to crack or brute-force strong encryption.

steps.title: Work out which encryption it is
steps.detail: On Windows it is often BitLocker. On Mac it is FileVault. Others include VeraCrypt or LUKS on Linux. Each has its own unlock method.

steps.title: Find your recovery key
steps.detail: BitLocker keys are often saved to your Microsoft account (account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey), a work or school account, a printout, or a USB stick. FileVault can use your Apple Account or a recovery key you saved.

steps.title: Check old notes and password managers
steps.detail: Search email, password managers, printed pages, and cloud storage for a long number or phrase. A recovery key is usually a 48-digit number for BitLocker.

steps.title: Unlock a healthy drive and copy the files
steps.detail: Use the key to unlock the drive in the normal system, then copy your files to a different drive.

steps.title: If the drive is also failing, image it first
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to make a raw copy of the encrypted drive to another drive. You can unlock the copy later with the key. Do not decrypt or repair the original.

steps.title: Accept the limit if no key exists
steps.detail: Without the password or recovery key, modern encryption cannot be reasonably broken. Recovery tools like PhotoRec will only return scrambled data.

encrypted.callPro: If the drive is also failing or damaged and you hold the key, a professional can image it for you. Without the key, no one can realistically recover the data.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker recovery key?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, or in a work or school account, a printed page, or a saved file or USB stick.

faq.q: Can someone crack the encryption for me?
faq.a: Not realistically. Modern encryption with a strong password is built to resist this, so be careful of anyone who says otherwise.

faq.q: What if I forgot my FileVault password?
faq.a: Try your Apple Account reset or the recovery key you saved when you turned it on. Without those, the data cannot be unlocked.
